subproblem.title: Differentiation under the integral sign: d/dt ∫ g(t⁻¹y) dμ(y) = −t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y)
subproblem.statement: Let μ be a Borel measure on ℝ^N that is finite on compact sets and let g : ℝ^N → ℝ be a C¹ function with compact support, Dg = fderiv ℝ g. Then for every t > 0 the function r ↦ ∫ g(r⁻¹y) dμ(y) on ℝ (with the convention 0⁻¹ = 0, as in Lean; only its values near t matter) is differentiable at t with derivative −(t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y)).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Euclidean N)), IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ → ∀ g : Euclidean N → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ 1 g → HasCompactSupport g → ∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → HasDerivAt (fun r : ℝ => ∫ y, g (r⁻¹ • y) ∂μ) (-(t⁻¹ * ∫ y, fderiv ℝ g (t⁻¹ • y) (t⁻¹ • y) ∂μ)) t
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: steps 0, 1, 4 and 5 of the parent proof (pointwise t-derivative and differentiation under the integral sign), with all constants explicit.
Hypotheses: μ is a measure on ℝ^N = Euclidean N (Borel σ-algebra) with μ(K) < ∞ for every compact K (IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ); g : ℝ^N → ℝ is C¹ with compact support; Dg := fderiv ℝ g. Fix t > 0. We prove that r ↦ ∫ g(r⁻¹y) dμ(y) has derivative −(t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y)) at t.
1. (Integrability principle.) Every continuous f : ℝ^N → ℝ with compact support is μ-integrable (Continuous.integrable_of_hasCompactSupport, using IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ).
2. (Constants.) tsupport g is compact, hence bounded: choose R₀ with tsupport g ⊆ B_{R₀}(0) (closed ball) and put R := max(R₀, 1), so R ≥ 1 > 0 and tsupport g ⊆ B_R(0). Since g is C¹, g is differentiable everywhere and Dg is continuous (ContDiff.differentiable, ContDiff.continuous_fderiv). Dg vanishes outside tsupport g (fderiv_of_notMem_tsupport), so Dg has compact support (HasCompactSupport.fderiv) and, being continuous, is bounded (Continuous.bounded_above_of_compact_support): choose L with ‖Dg(y)‖ ≤ L for all y; then L ≥ ‖Dg(0)‖ ≥ 0.
3. (Pointwise r-derivative.) Fix y ∈ ℝ^N and r > 0. The map ρ ↦ ρ⁻¹ has derivative −(r²)⁻¹ at ρ = r (hasDerivAt_inv, r ≠ 0), so ρ ↦ ρ⁻¹·y has derivative (−(r²)⁻¹)·y at ρ = r (HasDerivAt.smul_const). As g is differentiable at r⁻¹y, the chain rule (HasFDerivAt.comp_hasDerivAt) shows that ρ ↦ g(ρ⁻¹y) has derivative Dg(r⁻¹y)((−(r²)⁻¹)·y) at ρ = r. By linearity of Dg(r⁻¹y), Dg(r⁻¹y)((−(r²)⁻¹)·y) = −(r²)⁻¹·Dg(r⁻¹y)(y) = −(r⁻¹·(r⁻¹·Dg(r⁻¹y)(y))) = −(r⁻¹·Dg(r⁻¹y)(r⁻¹y)). Writing Φ(r,y) := −(r⁻¹·Dg(r⁻¹y)(r⁻¹y)), we conclude: for every y and every r > 0, ρ ↦ g(ρ⁻¹y) has derivative Φ(r,y) at ρ = r.
4. (Neighbourhood and dominating function.) Let I := (t/2, 2t). Since t/2 < t < 2t, I is an open interval containing t, hence a neighbourhood of t (Ioo_mem_nhds), and every r ∈ I satisfies r > t/2 > 0. Define b(y) := 2LR/t if ‖y‖ ≤ 2tR and b(y) := 0 otherwise, i.e. b is the indicator of the closed ball B_{2tR}(0) times the constant 2LR/t; b ≥ 0 because L ≥ 0, R > 0 and t > 0.
5. (Domination.) Let y ∈ ℝ^N and r ∈ I; we show |Φ(r,y)| ≤ b(y). Case r⁻¹y ∉ tsupport g: then Dg(r⁻¹y) = 0 (fderiv_of_notMem_tsupport), so Φ(r,y) = 0 ≤ b(y). Case r⁻¹y ∈ tsupport g: then ‖r⁻¹y‖ ≤ R; since y = r·(r⁻¹y) and r > 0, ‖y‖ = r·‖r⁻¹y‖ ≤ r·R ≤ 2t·R (as r < 2t and R > 0), so y ∈ B_{2tR}(0) and b(y) = 2LR/t. Moreover |Dg(r⁻¹y)(r⁻¹y)| ≤ ‖Dg(r⁻¹y)‖·‖r⁻¹y‖ ≤ L·R (operator-norm bound, using L ≥ 0), and 0 < r⁻¹ ≤ (t/2)⁻¹ = 2/t because r ≥ t/2 > 0 (inv_anti₀). Therefore |Φ(r,y)| = r⁻¹·|Dg(r⁻¹y)(r⁻¹y)| ≤ (2/t)·(L·R) = 2LR/t = b(y).
6. (Integrability and measurability.) (a) b is μ-integrable: the closed ball B_{2tR}(0) is measurable and compact, hence of finite μ-measure, so the constant 2LR/t is integrable on it (integrableOn_const) and its indicator b is integrable (integrable_indicator_iff). (b) For every r ∈ ℝ (with 0⁻¹ = 0), y ↦ g(r⁻¹y) is continuous (composition of g with the continuous map y ↦ r⁻¹y), hence a.e. strongly measurable. (c) y ↦ g(t⁻¹y) is continuous with compact support (HasCompactSupport.comp_smul, t⁻¹ ≠ 0), hence μ-integrable by step 1. (d) y ↦ Φ(t,y) = −(t⁻¹·Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y)) is continuous (Dg is continuous; Continuous.clm_apply), hence a.e. strongly measurable.
7. (Dominated differentiation.) Apply Mathlib's hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le (Analysis/Calculus/ParametricIntegral.lean:286) with F(r,y) := g(r⁻¹y), F'(r,y) := Φ(r,y), base point t, neighbourhood I and bound b. Its hypotheses are: step 6(b) (F(r,·) is a.e. strongly measurable for r near t), step 6(c) (F(t,·) is integrable), step 6(d) (F'(t,·) is a.e. strongly measurable), step 5 (for every y and every r ∈ I, ‖F'(r,y)‖ ≤ b(y)), step 6(a) (b is integrable), and step 3 (for every y and every r ∈ I, ρ ↦ F(ρ,y) has derivative F'(r,y) at ρ = r, valid since r > 0). It yields that r ↦ ∫ g(r⁻¹y) dμ(y) has derivative ∫ Φ(t,y) dμ(y) at t.
8. (Rewriting the derivative.) ∫ Φ(t,y) dμ(y) = ∫ −(t⁻¹·Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y)) dμ(y) = −∫ t⁻¹·Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y) = −(t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y)), by integral_neg and integral_const_mul (both valid without integrability hypotheses). Hence r ↦ ∫ g(r⁻¹y) dμ(y) has derivative −(t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ(y)) at t. ∎
proof_key_steps: Fix R > 0 with tsupport g ⊆ B_R(0) and L ≥ 0 with ‖Dg‖ ≤ L (Dg continuous with compact support).
For y fixed and r > 0, ρ ↦ g(ρ⁻¹y) has derivative Φ(r,y) = −(r⁻¹·Dg(r⁻¹y)(r⁻¹y)) at ρ = r (hasDerivAt_inv, smul_const, chain rule, linearity).
On I = (t/2, 2t), |Φ(r,y)| ≤ b(y) := (2LR/t)·1_{B_{2tR}(0)}(y), which is μ-integrable (compact ball, finite measure).
hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le gives derivative ∫ Φ(t,y) dμ at t; integral_neg and integral_const_mul rewrite it as −(t⁻¹·∫ Dg(t⁻¹y)(t⁻¹y) dμ).

audit.reason: The prose and Lean type agree, including the total inverse convention. The pointwise derivative and its sign are correct. Compact support supplies R and a global derivative bound L; on (t/2,2t), the stated closed-ball indicator dominates the derivative uniformly and is integrable. Every measurability, integrability and neighbourhood hypothesis of the pinned dominated-differentiation theorem is supplied. Integral linearity gives exactly the stated derivative. The proof is complete and independent of the Euler identity and other children.
